full_judgment:
9. She lastly submits that as per section 27(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, the accused shall have to rebut presumption about the allegations and explain her position as to the acquisition of properties disclosing the sources of the income during trial of the case and on that landscape, the order of discharge on the basis of defence materials and on mere denial of allegations by the accused, cannot sustain in the eye of law and on that panorama of the fact, the impugned order should be set-aside. The learned Advocate in support of her contentions has cited decisions in the cases of Abdul Wahab (Md) vs State, reported in 18 BLC 382 wherein it was held that the accused can rebut the presumption of acquisition of properties which are disproportionate to her known source of income during trial of the case and Sabira Sultana vs State, reported in 19 BLC 349 wherein it was decided that the accused is under the legal obligation to clear her position and account for in respect of the possession of the property allegedly disproportionate to her known sources of income to the satisfaction of the Court. 

 21. It transpires from the FIR and charge-sheet that there are specific allegations against the accused that she was owning and possessing some properties which are alleged to be disproportionate to her known sources of income. It is necessary to spell out as to how she acquired those properties. Therefore, the accused is liable to rebut presumption in the Court during the trial as contemplated under section 27(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. If the trial is not allowed to be held, it would not be possible to ascertain as to whether the property acquired by the accused is disproportionate to her legal sources of income or not. It is also necessary to ascertain the source of money of the accused for the acquisition of those properties. It is contended on behalf of the accused that the money/excess as alleged in the FIR is a marginal one which cannot be considered disproportionate to her known sources of income. The learned Advocate for the accused in support of his contention has cited a decision in the case Krishnanand Agnihotri vs State of MP, reported in AIR 1977 Supreme Court 796 which arose out of conviction and sentence but the present case at hand is at the initial stage and it was held therein that since the excess was comparatively small-it was less than ten percent of the total income of Rs. 1,27,715.43- it would not be right to hold that the assets found in the possession of the accused were disproportionate to his known sources of income so as to justify the raising of presumption with regard to the offences. Now question arises as to whether the money/excess as alleged in the FIR is a small one of the total income of the accused or not. The aforesaid matter can be looked into by the learned trial judge during trial of the case since it is also a disputed question of facts to be resolved on taking evidence from the respective parties. So at this stage, it cannot be said that the money/excess as disclosed in the FIR is small/marginal amount of money of the total income of the accused. Accordingly, we are not at one with the submission of the learned Advocate for the accused on this issue. It is argued on behalf of the accused that the accused paid income tax upon assessment of income derived from the properties and the same was accepted by the income tax department and for this reason, the present case filed against the accused disputing the value of properties, liabilities and expenditures and cost of construction is not maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law. Before coming to a decision in this matter, we feel it convenient to know about the purpose and object of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 and the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. The purpose and object of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 is to realize income-tax in respect of the total income of the income year or income years as the case may be of every person. 

 24. Under the circumstances, we are of the view that acceptance of income tax return by the Income Tax Department does not create any legal bar to bring allegations against the accused under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 and the accused-petitioner shall get scope to rebut presumption as to correctness of the allegations before the court under section 27(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004.
